hook: You feel a rush when you hear a catchy tune.

sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You feel a rush when you hear a catchy tune. That rush actually mirrors a behavior recorded centuries ago in marine mammals. In 2011, Dr. Diana Reiss at Emory University noted about 30% more whistles during dolphin excitement. The result? The whistles signaled joyful bursts, not aggression. Other studies with wild pods in the Bahamas found the same pattern. Captive groups in Japan showed identical vocal spikes. Scientists call this social laughter. Researchers also observed dolphins leaping together during these moments. These leaps often align with the peak of their vocal bursts. The behavior suggests a shared emotional language across species. So why do we think only humans can feel that burst of happiness? Because research shows both species share the same brain reward circuits. What did the researchers actually measure? They counted increased whistle rates and longer interaction times. Does it still hold today? Modern observations confirm dolphins still celebrate with vocal spikes when surfing waves. That's it. So next time you hum a happy tune, remember your brain echoes dolphin splash. You feel a rush

claims.claim: Dolphins increase signature whistle rates by about 30% during excitement
Synchronized leaps were documented among wild bottlenose dolphins during social excitement
